Governments measure their value through graduate employment rates, research income and patents, while students increasingly view a degree as a financial investment whose return must be calculated.

This vocational turn has provoked sharp debate. Proponents argue that universities must remain relevant to a changing labour market and that equipping students with practical skills is a legitimate public duty. Critics respond that this narrow emphasis erodes the humanities, discourages risky or unfashionable research, and turns education into mere training. They warn that a society which values only immediately useful knowledge may lose the capacity for the deeper, slower thinking on which genuine innovation depends.

The tension is unlikely to be resolved quickly. Most observers agree that universities must serve both purposes, yet finding a balance between intellectual freedom and economic utility remains among the most contested questions in contemporary higher education.

ielts-r02.title: Bilingual Education and Cognitive Development
ielts-r02.text:
For much of the twentieth century, many educators believed that learning two languages in childhood confused the developing mind and slowed academic progress. Children who spoke a minority language at home were often discouraged from using it at school, on the assumption that the mother tongue interfered with mastery of the dominant language.

Research over recent decades has largely overturned this view. Studies comparing bilingual and monolingual children have found that bilinguals frequently outperform their peers on tasks requiring attention, switching between activities and ignoring irrelevant information. These are components of executive function, the mental processes that allow people to plan, focus and control impulses. Because bilinguals constantly suppress one language while using another, they appear to develop stronger cognitive control, a benefit that may persist into old age and even delay the onset of dementia.

Sceptics point out that the effects are modest and not universal, and that social class, parental education and teaching quality complicate the picture. Nonetheless, the consensus has shifted decisively. Bilingualism is now widely viewed not as a handicap but as an asset, and many school systems that once suppressed minority languages now promote them through dual-language programmes.

ielts-r03.title: The Rise of Massive Open Online Courses
ielts-r03.text:
Few educational innovations have generated as much enthusiasm, and as much disappointment, as the massive open online course, or MOOC. When prestigious universities began offering free online courses to unlimited numbers of learners in 2012, many commentators predicted a revolution: education would be democratised, and anyone with an internet connection could study with the best teachers in the world.

A decade later the picture is more sober. Enrolment figures remain enormous, but completion rates are strikingly low, often below ten per cent. Many registrants never begin, and most who start drift away within weeks. Researchers attribute this to the absence of deadlines, the lack of face-to-face support and the difficulty of sustaining motivation without a peer group or a teacher who knows your name.

Yet it would be wrong to dismiss the MOOC entirely. For self-directed professionals seeking specific skills, for learners in regions with limited access to higher education, and for institutions experimenting with blended teaching, the model has delivered real value. Rather than replacing universities, MOOCs have largely been absorbed into them, becoming tools that traditional providers use to extend their reach rather than rivals that threaten their existence.

ielts-r04.title: Standardised Testing and Its Critics
ielts-r04.text:
Standardised tests have become a central feature of education systems around the world. Their advocates value them as objective, comparable and efficient instruments for measuring achievement, holding schools accountable and identifying pupils who need extra help. Because every student answers the same questions under the same conditions, the results appear to offer a fair basis for comparison.

Critics, however, argue that this fairness is largely an illusion. They contend that such tests measure only a narrow slice of ability, favouring quick recall and test-taking skill over creativity, critical thinking and deep understanding. Because the results carry high stakes, teachers are pressured to teach to the test, narrowing the curriculum and squeezing out subjects such as art and music. Poorer schools, critics add, often lack the resources to prepare students effectively, so tests can entrench rather than reveal inequality.

The dispute has no easy resolution. Both sides can point to evidence, and much depends on how scores are used. Few would argue that assessment itself is unnecessary; the real question is whether a single timed examination should carry so much weight, or whether a richer mixture of methods would give a truer picture of what students can do.

ielts-r05.title: Early Childhood Education and Long-Term Outcomes
ielts-r05.text:
The first five years of life are a period of extraordinary brain development, and educators and economists alike have become increasingly interested in what happens during this window. High-quality early childhood education, which combines structured play, language-rich interaction and sensitive caregiving, has been shown to produce benefits that persist for decades.

The most famous evidence comes from longitudinal studies such as the Perry Preschool Project, which followed disadvantaged children into adulthood. Participants were more likely to finish school, to be employed and to own homes, and less likely to be arrested, than a control group. Follow-up calculations suggested that every dollar invested returned several dollars in reduced social costs and higher productivity.

Yet enthusiasm must be tempered by realism. The strongest results come from intensive, well-staffed programmes, and cheaper, lower-quality provision may deliver little. Access also remains uneven, with the children who would benefit most often least likely to receive places. Policymakers therefore face a choice: invest seriously in quality, or spend less and risk the appearance of action without its substance. The evidence increasingly suggests that the earlier society invests, and the higher the quality it funds, the greater the return.

ielts-r06.title: The Science of Climate Change
ielts-r06.text:
The scientific consensus on climate change is among the strongest in the history of science. Measurements from ice cores, tree rings, weather stations and satellites all point to the same conclusion: the planet is warming, and human activity is the principal cause. The mechanism is well understood. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, which trap heat in the atmosphere that would otherwise escape into space.

There is no serious scientific dispute about the basic physics, which has been understood since the nineteenth century. What remains uncertain is the precise scale and speed of the changes to come. Climate models can project broad trends, but the behaviour of clouds, oceans and polar ice introduces uncertainty, and the difference between a rise of one and a half degrees and three degrees is enormous in human terms.

This genuine uncertainty is frequently exploited by those who wish to delay action, who argue that because scientists cannot predict exactly what will happen, nothing should be done. Most scientists regard this as a dangerous confusion of two very different questions. That the climate is changing is established fact; precisely how quickly and how severely is a matter of informed estimation. Neither is a reason for inaction.

ielts-r07.title: Plastic Pollution in the Oceans
ielts-r07.text:
The durability that makes plastic so useful also makes it one of the most persistent pollutants on Earth. Millions of tonnes of plastic waste enter the oceans each year, where it can survive for centuries. Large items entangle marine animals, while smaller fragments are mistaken for food and ingested, blocking digestive tracts and concentrating toxic chemicals.

Particular concern has focused on microplastics, particles smaller than five millimetres that arise from the breakdown of larger items and from sources such as synthetic clothing and cosmetics. These particles are now found from the deepest ocean trenches to Arctic sea ice, and they have entered the food chain in ways scientists are only beginning to understand. Laboratory studies have shown harmful effects on marine organisms, though the implications for human health remain less clear.

The solutions are as much economic and political as technical. Improved waste management, reductions in single-use packaging and the development of biodegradable alternatives all have a role. Yet recycling alone cannot keep pace with rising production, and many experts argue that the only durable answer is to reduce the amount of plastic produced in the first place, a step that requires producers and governments, not just consumers, to act.

ielts-r08.title: Deforestation and Biodiversity Loss
ielts-r08.text:
Tropical forests cover only a small fraction of the Earth's surface, yet they are home to more than half of all terrestrial species. This extraordinary concentration of life makes deforestation one of the greatest threats to global biodiversity. When forest is cleared for agriculture, cattle pasture or timber, species lose their habitat, and many that are found nowhere else disappear, often before scientists have even described them.

The causes of deforestation are economic. In many tropical countries, clearing land for soy, palm oil or beef is more profitable, at least in the short term, than preserving forest. Weak governance, unclear land tenure and global demand for commodities all accelerate the process. Conservationists argue that forests must be valued for the services they provide, including carbon storage, water regulation and the preservation of genetic resources, not merely for the timber or farmland they can yield.

International efforts have produced mixed results. Some countries have sharply reduced deforestation through a combination of enforcement, satellite monitoring and payments to landowners. Elsewhere, losses continue at alarming rates. The challenge is to make conservation pay, so that the communities living in and around forests have a stake in their survival rather than an incentive to destroy them.

ielts-r09.title: Renewable Energy and the Transition from Fossil Fuels
ielts-r09.text:
The transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy is the most consequential industrial change of the twenty-first century. Solar and wind power, once expensive novelties, are now among the cheapest sources of electricity in many parts of the world, and their costs continue to fall. This rapid improvement has transformed the economics of energy and raised hopes that emissions can be cut quickly enough to avoid the worst effects of climate change.

Yet the transition is not straightforward. The sun does not always shine and the wind does not always blow, so systems must store energy or retain backup capacity, both of which add cost. The minerals needed for batteries, solar panels and wind turbines are concentrated in a small number of countries, creating new dependencies. And the social consequences are uneven: regions built on coal, oil and gas face job losses that must be managed if the transition is to be politically sustainable.

Few serious analysts doubt that the destination is renewable. The question is how fast the journey can be made, and at what cost to whom. A transition that is rapid but unjust may prove no more durable than one that is slow. Success will depend not only on technology but on the politics of sharing its burdens and benefits.

ielts-r10.title: Water Scarcity in a Warming World
ielts-r10.text:
Fresh water is essential to life, yet it is distributed very unevenly across the planet, and climate change is widening the gap between supply and demand. Rising temperatures increase evaporation, alter rainfall patterns and shrink the glaciers and snowpacks that feed many of the world's great rivers. At the same time, growing populations, expanding agriculture and industrial development are consuming ever larger quantities of water.

The consequences are already visible. Rivers that once reached the sea now dry up before doing so. Aquifers, the underground reservoirs that supply a third of humanity, are being depleted faster than they can be replenished. Competition for scarce water fuels tensions between farmers, cities and neighbouring countries, and the poor, who depend most directly on rivers and rain, are hit hardest.

Addressing scarcity requires more than building dams or drilling deeper wells, which often make matters worse in the long run. Experts emphasise efficiency, including the repair of leaking pipes, the adoption of drip irrigation and the reuse of wastewater. Pricing water realistically, so that it is not wasted, is also essential. Above all, they argue, water must be understood as a finite and shared resource whose careful management is a condition of survival in a warming world.

ielts-r11.title: The Obesity Epidemic
ielts-r11.text:
Obesity has tripled worldwide since 1975, and no country has succeeded in reversing the trend. Once regarded as a problem of wealthy nations, it is now rising fastest in low and middle income countries, where undernutrition and obesity increasingly coexist within the same communities and even the same households.

The causes are systemic rather than purely personal. Diets have shifted towards cheap, energy-dense processed foods that are heavily marketed and widely available, while physical activity has declined as work and transport have become more sedentary. In this environment, individual willpower alone is rarely enough, and framing obesity as a simple matter of personal failure misunderstands the problem.

Public health experts therefore favour policies that change the environment rather than merely lecturing individuals. Taxes on sugary drinks, restrictions on advertising to children, clearer food labelling and urban design that encourages walking and cycling have all been shown to have some effect. None is a magic bullet, and the food industry has vigorously resisted regulation. Yet the alternative, continuing to treat a largely environmental problem as if it were only a matter of character, has so far produced nothing but worsening statistics.

ielts-r12.title: Antibiotic Resistance
ielts-r12.text:
Antibiotics are among the greatest discoveries in medical history, transforming infections that were once routinely fatal into minor ailments. But their effectiveness is being steadily eroded by resistance, the process by which bacteria evolve to survive drugs designed to kill them. Every use of an antibiotic gives resistant strains a survival advantage, and the more the drugs are used, the faster resistance spreads.

The problem is aggravated by misuse. In many countries antibiotics can be bought without prescription and are taken for viral illnesses against which they are useless. In agriculture, huge quantities are given to healthy animals to promote growth, exposing billions of bacteria to the drugs and allowing resistance genes to enter the human food chain.

The consequences are alarming. Routine operations and cancer treatments, which rely on antibiotics to prevent infection, could become far more dangerous, and the world may return to an era in which minor wounds are life-threatening. The development of new antibiotics has slowed to a trickle because they are less profitable than drugs taken for life. Combating resistance therefore requires not only new medicines but stricter controls on how existing ones are used, in both human and veterinary medicine.

ielts-r13.title: Mental Health and the Modern Workplace
ielts-r13.text:
Mental health has moved from the margins of public debate to its centre, and the workplace is a major focus of concern. Employers have begun to recognise that stress, anxiety and depression are not merely private troubles but impose real costs in lost productivity, absenteeism and staff turnover. In response, many organisations now offer counselling services, flexible working and training for managers in how to support struggling employees.

Yet critics detect a gap between rhetoric and reality. While companies advertise their commitment to wellbeing, workloads have in many cases continued to rise, and the root causes of poor mental health, including long hours, job insecurity and unrealistic targets, remain untouched. Offering yoga classes or meditation apps, however welcome, does little if the underlying demands are unsustainable. Some observers argue that wellness programmes serve mainly to shift responsibility from the employer to the individual, implying that the problem lies in the worker's resilience rather than in the working conditions.

The deeper question is whether workplaces can be redesigned so that they sustain rather than exhaust the people who work in them. This would require more than gestures: it would mean rethinking how work is organised, measured and rewarded.

ielts-r14.title: Vaccination and Herd Immunity
ielts-r14.text:
Vaccination is widely regarded as one of the most effective public health interventions ever devised. It has eradicated smallpox, driven polio to the brink of extinction and dramatically reduced the toll of diseases such as measles. The principle is simple: by exposing the immune system to a harmless form of a pathogen, a vaccine teaches the body to recognise and defeat the real thing before it can cause serious harm.

Vaccines protect not only the individual but the community, through a phenomenon known as herd immunity. When a sufficiently high proportion of a population is immune, a disease cannot spread easily, and those who cannot be vaccinated, including infants, the elderly and people with weakened immune systems, are shielded. The threshold required varies by disease; for measles, among the most contagious known, coverage of around ninety-five per cent is needed.

The remarkable success of vaccination has, paradoxically, weakened public appreciation of it. Diseases that once terrified parents are now rare, so the threat seems distant, and unfounded fears about safety have discouraged some from vaccinating their children. When coverage falls below the herd immunity threshold, outbreaks return. Public health authorities therefore face a continual task: reminding a fortunate generation why the protection it takes for granted was won, and why it must be maintained.

ielts-r15.title: The Health Benefits of Physical Activity
ielts-r15.text:
Modern life has engineered physical effort out of daily routine. People sit at desks, commute by car and relax in front of screens, and the consequences for health are profound. Physical inactivity is now recognised as a major risk factor for heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and several cancers, comparable in its toll to smoking.

Yet the remedy is, in principle, simple and cheap. Regular moderate activity, such as brisk walking, cycling or gardening, brings substantial benefits. It strengthens the heart, helps control weight, improves mood and sleep, and reduces the risk of chronic disease. The World Health Organisation recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week for adults, and even smaller amounts, for those who are currently inactive, bring measurable gains.

The difficulty lies not in knowing what to do but in doing it. Exercise competes with many other demands on time, and for many people the built environment offers few opportunities for incidental activity, with no safe places to walk or cycle. This is why experts increasingly frame the problem as environmental rather than purely personal. Designing towns that make movement the easy choice, through pavements, cycle lanes and accessible parks, may do more for public health than any number of exhortations to hit the gym.

ielts-r16.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work
ielts-r16.text:
Few technologies inspire more excitement, and more anxiety, than artificial intelligence. Systems that can write, translate, analyse data and even produce images have advanced rapidly, and their creators promise that they will relieve humans of drudgery and boost productivity. But the same capabilities raise an uncomfortable question: if machines can perform tasks once reserved for educated professionals, what will be left for people to do?

History offers some reassurance. Every wave of automation, from the steam engine to the spreadsheet, destroyed some jobs while creating others, and overall employment grew. Optimists argue that AI will follow this pattern, eliminating routine tasks while generating new roles we cannot yet imagine. Pessimists reply that this time may be different, because AI is encroaching on cognitive work, not just manual labour, and because the new jobs it creates may demand skills that many displaced workers do not possess.

The honest answer is that the outcome is not predetermined. It will depend on choices about education, regulation and the distribution of gains. If societies invest in retraining and ensure that productivity gains are shared, AI could raise living standards broadly. If they do not, its benefits may flow to a narrow few while insecurity spreads.

ielts-r17.title: The Ethics of Data Collection
ielts-r17.text:
Every search, purchase and online interaction leaves a digital trace, and companies have become extraordinarily skilled at collecting and analysing these traces. This data powers services that are often free to the user, and it enables advertising that is targeted with remarkable precision. The bargain seems simple: convenience and free content in exchange for information about our habits and preferences.

But the bargain is more one-sided than it first appears. Most people have little idea what data is collected, how it is used or with whom it is shared, and the consent they give, usually by clicking through lengthy terms they have not read, is of doubtful value. Data can be used to infer intimate details, to manipulate behaviour, and to discriminate, for example by charging different prices to different people. When it falls into the wrong hands, or when it leaks, the consequences can be severe.

Regulators have begun to respond, most notably with the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, which grants individuals rights over their data and imposes penalties for misuse. Such rules are a start, but technology moves faster than legislation. The deeper challenge is to design systems in which privacy is the default, so that people do not have to surrender control of their lives to use the modern world.

ielts-r18.title: The Digital Divide
ielts-r18.text:
The internet was once hailed as a great leveller, a tool that would give everyone access to the same information and opportunities regardless of where they lived or how much they earned. To a degree that promise has been fulfilled: a student in a remote village can now attend lectures given thousands of miles away, and a small business can sell to customers on the other side of the world.

Yet access to the internet is far from universal, and the gap between the connected and the unconnected has profound consequences. In wealthy countries broadband is fast, cheap and taken for granted; in many poorer regions it is slow, expensive or absent altogether. This digital divide follows older divisions of geography and income, and it is increasingly self-reinforcing, because so many services, from education and banking to health care and government, have migrated online. Those who are offline are shut out not merely from entertainment but from participation in the economy and society itself.

Bridging the divide is not simply a matter of laying cables, though infrastructure is essential. Affordability, digital literacy and locally relevant content matter equally. Without them, connection alone may do little, and the risk is that the digital economy will compound existing inequalities rather than dissolve them.

ielts-r19.title: Social Media and Public Discourse
ielts-r19.text:
Social media platforms were launched with the promise of connecting people and giving everyone a voice, and in many ways they have delivered. Marginalised groups have found audiences, social movements have organised at speed, and ordinary citizens can hold the powerful to account in ways that were once unthinkable.

But the same architecture that enables these achievements also creates problems. Platforms optimise for engagement, and engagement is often driven by outrage, which travels fastest and farthest. Algorithms that reward strong emotion tend to amplify extreme and misleading content, while measured, complex arguments struggle for attention. Users are increasingly sorted into groups that see only what they already agree with, and the result is a public sphere that is more polarised and less capable of the shared, factual discussion on which democracy depends.

There is no consensus on the remedy. Proposals range from requiring platforms to moderate more aggressively to breaking up the largest companies, and each raises difficult questions about free speech and who should decide what is acceptable. What is increasingly clear is that the problem cannot be left to solve itself, because the incentives that shape these systems point in the wrong direction.

ielts-r20.title: The Attention Economy
ielts-r20.text:
In the digital age, human attention has become a scarce and valuable resource, and an entire industry has grown up around capturing and selling it. Every app, website and platform competes for the same finite quantity: the hours and minutes of our waking lives. The business models of the largest technology companies depend on holding our attention long enough to show us advertisements, and they have become extremely good at doing so.

The techniques are sophisticated. Notifications arrive at carefully chosen moments, feeds are designed to be endless, and content is selected by algorithms that learn precisely what will keep each individual scrolling. Designers speak openly of creating habits, and the language of addiction is increasingly applied to the results. Many users report wanting to spend less time on their devices but finding themselves unable to stop.

This has prompted a backlash. Features that limit screen time, the rise of distraction-free software and a growing literature on digital wellbeing all testify to a spreading unease. Yet the underlying incentives are unchanged: attention remains profitable. Until the economics of attention are reformed, critics argue, individuals will continue to fight an uneven battle against systems engineered, by some of the brightest minds available, to be irresistible.

ielts-r21.title: The Growth of Megacities
ielts-r21.text:
For the first time in history, more than half of humanity lives in cities, and a growing share lives in megacities, metropolitan areas with more than ten million inhabitants. This concentration of people is often portrayed as a source of opportunity: cities are engines of innovation and growth, and their density allows services to be provided efficiently to large numbers of people.

Yet the sheer scale of the largest cities creates formidable problems. Housing is scarce and expensive, transport networks are overwhelmed, and air and water pollution exact a heavy toll on health. Many megacities are located in developing countries where infrastructure has not kept pace with growth, and millions of residents live in informal settlements that lack sanitation and secure tenure. The gap between the gleaming business districts and the sprawling periphery is often stark.

The challenge is therefore one of management as much as of growth. Some cities have shown that careful planning, investment in public transport and policies that encourage mixed-income neighbourhoods can make density liveable. Others risk becoming divided, congested and unmanageable. As the urban population continues to swell, how the world's megacities are governed may determine whether urbanisation proves to be a blessing or a burden.

ielts-r22.title: Urban Sprawl and Its Consequences
ielts-r22.text:
As cities grow, they do not always grow up; very often they grow out. Urban sprawl, the spread of low-density development over previously rural land, is a dominant feature of cities in many countries, particularly those where land is cheap and the car is king.

The appeal of sprawl is easy to understand. Houses on the suburban fringe are larger and more affordable than those in the centre, and residents enjoy gardens, quiet streets and cleaner air. These are genuine benefits, and millions of people have chosen them willingly.

The costs, however, are spread across society. Sprawl depends on the car: distances are too great for walking or cycling, and public transport is hard to provide efficiently where homes are thinly scattered. The result is long commutes, heavy traffic and dependence on cheap fuel. Low-density development also consumes farmland and natural habitat, and it costs more per household to serve with roads, sewers and schools than compact development does. Perhaps most troubling, sprawl has been linked to poorer health, since car-dependent residents walk less and sit more.

Planners increasingly favour denser, more compact cities where homes, jobs and services are close together. But changing direction is hard once the pattern is set, because roads, zoning and expectations all point the other way.

ielts-r23.title: Affordable Housing in Growing Cities
ielts-r23.text:
In successful cities, land is scarce and prices are high, and this creates a problem that affects everyone but falls hardest on those with the least: the shortage of affordable housing. As cities attract workers and investment, demand for homes near jobs and services pushes rents and purchase prices beyond the reach of teachers, nurses, cleaners and young families.

The causes are disputed. Some blame restrictive planning rules that make it difficult to build densely enough, so supply fails to keep pace with demand. Others point to the financialisation of housing, the treatment of homes as investment assets to be bought and sold for profit, which drives up prices and leaves properties empty while people sleep rough. In many cities both forces operate together.

The consequences extend beyond housing itself. When workers cannot afford to live near their jobs, they face punishing commutes or move away, and employers struggle to recruit. Cities that once mixed rich and poor become segregated, and the services that depend on a diverse workforce begin to fray.

There is no single solution. Most experts agree that cities need to build more, and more densely, while also protecting tenants and investing directly in social housing. The difficulty is political: those who already own homes often benefit from scarcity and resist change.

ielts-r24.title: Smart Cities and Urban Planning
ielts-r24.text:
The smart city is a seductive idea. By embedding sensors throughout the urban fabric and connecting them through data networks, cities can, its advocates claim, manage traffic in real time, reduce energy use, predict crime and respond to problems before they escalate. Streetlights that dim when no one is present, buses that adjust routes to demand, and systems that detect leaking pipes are all cited as examples of what technology can offer.

Critics urge caution. They note that the benefits of smart systems often flow to those who are already well served, while the needs of poorer residents, who may lack smartphones or internet access, are overlooked. There are also concerns about surveillance and privacy, since the sensors that make a city efficient also record where people go and what they do. And technology, however clever, cannot substitute for competent governance: a city with sensors but without the capacity to act on the data has bought an expensive ornament.

Supporters respond that these are reasons to design smart systems better, not to abandon them, and that data can make urban services fairer as well as more efficient, for example by revealing which neighbourhoods are underserved. The debate reflects a deeper question about who the city is for, and whether its tools should serve its citizens or merely monitor them.

ielts-r25.title: The Environmental Footprint of Cities
ielts-r25.text:
Cities are often blamed for environmental damage, and with some reason: they consume the great majority of the world's energy and produce most of its carbon emissions. Yet the relationship between urbanisation and the environment is more complex than this simple indictment suggests.

Dense cities can, in fact, be among the most efficient places for people to live. Apartment buildings need less heating and cooling per person than detached houses, and residents who can walk, cycle or take public transport generate far fewer emissions than those who must drive everywhere. Studies consistently find that city dwellers, particularly in compact, well-planned cities, have smaller carbon footprints than their rural and suburban counterparts.

The danger is not cities as such but the form they take. Sprawling, car-dependent cities are environmental disasters, while dense, transit-oriented ones can be relatively green. The difference lies in design and policy: in whether housing is built near jobs, whether public transport is fast and affordable, and whether streets are designed for people rather than vehicles.

The challenge is therefore not to abandon urbanisation, which no country is likely to do, but to shape it. The greenest city of the future may be the one that packs people close together and makes leaving the car at home the easiest choice.

ielts-r26.title: Globalisation and Cultural Homogenisation
ielts-r26.text:
Walk down the main street of almost any large city and you may struggle to tell which country you are in. The same coffee chains, clothing brands and fast-food outlets appear everywhere, and a casual observer might conclude that globalisation is steadily erasing cultural difference, replacing the world's rich variety with one uniform consumer culture.

There is some truth in this. The global reach of a few powerful companies does standardise tastes, and many local businesses have been displaced by international competitors with greater scale and marketing power. Languages, cuisines and traditions built over centuries can seem fragile in the face of this tide.

Yet the picture is not simply one of loss. Globalisation also spreads ideas, and cultures have always borrowed from one another. The result is often not uniformity but hybridity: Indian and Japanese influences reshape global cuisine even as global chains adapt their menus to local tastes. Moreover, the same networks that carry global brands also allow minority cultures to find audiences, so that musicians, writers and craftspeople who would once have been confined to a local market can now reach the world.

The real question is one of power. When exchange is equal, it enriches; when it is one-way, it threatens. The challenge is to keep cultural exchange a conversation rather than a monologue.

ielts-r27.title: Global Trade and Economic Interdependence
ielts-r27.text:
The volume of goods crossing national borders has grown spectacularly over the past half century. Falling transport costs, containerised shipping and the removal of trade barriers have woven national economies into a single, tightly linked system, in which a product may be designed in one country, assembled from parts made in several others and sold worldwide.

This integration has brought undeniable benefits. It has allowed countries to specialise in what they do best, lowered prices for consumers and lifted hundreds of millions of people out of poverty, particularly in Asia. No serious economist wishes to return to a world of closed borders and self-sufficiency.

But interdependence cuts both ways. When economies are tightly linked, a shock in one place travels quickly everywhere. The disruption of a single port or factory can ripple through global supply chains, as recent crises demonstrated when shortages of components halted production across industries. Dependence on a few suppliers also concentrates risk, and the system that delivers efficiency in good times can deliver fragility in bad ones.

Governments are now reconsidering the balance between efficiency and resilience. Some are encouraging production closer to home, holding larger stocks or diversifying suppliers, accepting somewhat higher costs in exchange for greater security. The era of maximum integration may be giving way to something more cautious.

ielts-r28.title: Migration in a Globalised World
ielts-r28.text:
People have always moved, but globalisation has made migration easier, cheaper and more visible than ever before. Falling travel costs, the spread of information about opportunities abroad and the demands of ageing economies have all encouraged people to cross borders in search of work, safety or a better life for their children.

The economic case for migration is, in broad terms, strong. Migrants fill labour shortages, pay taxes, start businesses and often do work that local populations are unwilling or unable to do. They also send remittances home, sums that in many developing countries exceed foreign aid and form a vital source of income for families left behind.

Yet migration is rarely a purely economic question. It raises difficult issues of identity, integration and national sovereignty, and in many receiving countries it has become one of the most divisive subjects in politics. Host societies may welcome the labour migrants provide while resenting their presence, a contradiction that fuels resentment on both sides.

There is no simple formula. The countries that manage migration best tend to combine openness to the workers they need with honest investment in integration, housing, language and education. The alternative, treating migrants as permanent outsiders, wastes their potential and stores up problems for the future.

ielts-r29.title: Multinational Corporations and Global Supply Chains
ielts-r29.text:
Multinational corporations are among the most powerful actors in the modern world, and their influence now rivals that of many governments. The largest operate in dozens of countries, command revenues greater than many national economies and shape billions of lives through the goods they produce and the jobs they provide.

Their power rests on the global supply chain, the network of suppliers and factories that stretches across continents. By locating each stage of production where it is cheapest, corporations have driven down prices and made a huge range of goods available to ordinary consumers. This efficiency, however, comes with costs that the price tag does not show.

Supply chains have often been criticised for poor working conditions, low wages and environmental damage in the countries where goods are made, problems that are obscured by distance and by the complexity of who is responsible for what. When a garment is stitched by a subcontractor of a subcontractor, accountability blurs, and corporations can claim ignorance of abuses they would never tolerate at home.

Efforts to impose responsibility, through auditing, certification and new laws requiring companies to monitor their supply chains, have grown. Whether such measures can tame firms whose reach exceeds the jurisdiction of any single state remains one of the open questions of the global era.

ielts-r30.title: Globalisation and Income Inequality
ielts-r30.text:
Has globalisation made the world more equal or less? The answer depends on where one looks, and the two most common views are, in a sense, both right.

Between countries, inequality has fallen dramatically. The rapid growth of China, India and other emerging economies, made possible in part by their integration into world trade, has lifted hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty and narrowed the gap between rich and poor nations for the first time in two centuries. This is among the great achievements of the era.

Within countries, however, the picture is often reversed. In many wealthy nations the gains from globalisation have flowed disproportionately to those with capital and advanced skills, while workers in manufacturing and routine jobs have seen their wages stagnate and their security erode. The result has been widening inequality and a sense, widespread in some communities, that the system is rigged in favour of a global elite.

These two trends are connected. The same forces that lifted incomes in emerging economies put downward pressure on wages in rich ones, and politicians who promise to reverse globalisation rarely acknowledge this trade-off. The task is not to choose between the two truths but to design policies, in taxation, education and social protection, that share the gains of openness more fairly within each country.

toefl-r01.title: The Double Helix of DNA
toefl-r01.text:
The discovery of the structure of deoxyribonucleic acid, or DNA, ranks among the most significant achievements in modern biology. In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick proposed that DNA takes the form of a double helix, a twisted ladder whose rungs are formed by pairs of chemical units called bases. Their model explained, for the first time, how genetic information could be stored and copied with remarkable fidelity.

The key insight was the pairing rule. Adenine always pairs with thymine, and guanine always pairs with cytosine. Because each strand of the helix complements the other, the molecule can separate into two templates, each of which directs the assembly of a new partner strand. This mechanism accounts for the faithful transmission of hereditary information from one generation to the next.

The implications were profound. Understanding DNA structure laid the foundation for molecular biology, enabling advances such as genetic engineering, forensic identification, and the mapping of entire genomes. Scientists could finally trace how traits are passed on and how errors in copying can lead to disease. Decades later, the human genome project built directly on this discovery.

toefl-r02.title: Plate Tectonics
toefl-r02.text:
The theory of plate tectonics explains how the surface of Earth is shaped. According to this theory, the outer shell of the planet is divided into several large, rigid plates that float slowly upon a partially molten layer beneath. These plates move only a few centimeters each year, yet over millions of years their motion has rearranged continents, raised mountain ranges, and opened and closed entire oceans.

The driving force behind this movement is heat from the interior of Earth. Convection currents in the mantle cause hot material to rise, spread sideways, and sink again, dragging the plates above. Where plates pull apart, new crust forms from molten rock; where they collide, one plate may slide beneath another, producing earthquakes and volcanoes. The Pacific Ring of Fire, for example, marks a boundary where such collisions are frequent.

The theory also explains the distribution of fossils and rocks. Matching formations found on continents now separated by oceans strongly suggest that these landmasses were once joined. Although the theory met resistance when it was proposed, the accumulation of evidence eventually made it the unifying framework of modern geology.

toefl-r03.title: Photosynthesis
toefl-r03.text:
Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy. Using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide, these organisms produce glucose and release oxygen as a byproduct. This reaction sustains nearly all life on Earth, either directly or indirectly, because it supplies both food and the oxygen that many organisms require to breathe.

The process occurs mainly in the chloroplasts of plant cells, where the pigment chlorophyll captures light. In the light-dependent stage, energy from the Sun splits water molecules, releasing oxygen and storing energy in chemical compounds. In the second stage, which does not require light, this stored energy is used to assemble carbon dioxide into glucose. The glucose can then be stored as starch or broken down to fuel the activities of the plant.

Human societies depend heavily on photosynthesis. Crops cultivated for food, forests that regulate the climate, and even the fossil fuels burned for energy all trace their origins to this ancient chemical pathway. Understanding it has helped scientists improve agricultural yields and explore ways to produce renewable fuels.

toefl-r04.title: The Theory of Evolution
toefl-r04.text:
The theory of evolution by natural selection, formulated by Charles Darwin in the nineteenth century, provides a unifying explanation for the diversity of life. Darwin observed that individual organisms within a species vary, and that many of these variations are inherited. He also noted that far more offspring are produced than can possibly survive, given limited food, space, and other resources.

From these observations, Darwin reasoned that individuals with traits better suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce. Over many generations, favorable traits become more common in a population, while less favorable ones diminish. Darwin called this process natural selection because the environment, rather than any deliberate choice, determines which individuals thrive. He gathered evidence from many fields, including fossils, the geographic distribution of species, and the selective breeding of domesticated animals.

The theory transformed biology. It explained how complex adaptations, such as the eye or the wing, could arise gradually through small, cumulative changes. Although Darwin lacked knowledge of genetics, later discoveries about DNA confirmed and extended his ideas, making evolution the central organizing principle of the life sciences.

toefl-r05.title: The Structure of the Atom
toefl-r05.text:
The modern understanding of the atom developed gradually over more than a century. Early models pictured the atom as a solid, indivisible sphere, but experiments in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries revealed a far more complex internal structure. Ernest Rutherford's famous gold-foil experiment, for instance, showed that most of an atom's mass is concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus at its center.

Later work refined this picture. The nucleus contains positively charged protons and neutral neutrons, while negatively charged electrons orbit at relatively vast distances from the center. Because atoms are mostly empty space, solid matter can pass through certain materials, and this explains a great deal about the behavior of matter. The number of protons, known as the atomic number, defines which element an atom is, while variations in the number of neutrons produce different isotopes of the same element.

Understanding atomic structure has had enormous consequences. It underlies chemistry, explains the properties of materials, and made possible technologies ranging from nuclear power to medical imaging. Yet the atom remains a subject of active research, as physicists continue to probe the behavior of particles smaller still.

toefl-r06.title: The Fall of the Roman Empire
toefl-r06.text:
The decline and fall of the Western Roman Empire is one of the most studied questions in history. For centuries, the empire dominated the Mediterranean world, but by the fifth century it had fragmented into a collection of successor kingdoms. Historians generally agree that no single cause explains this collapse; rather, a combination of pressures gradually undermined the imperial system.

Internal weaknesses played a major role. Political instability, with frequent changes of emperor and civil wars, weakened central authority. Economic troubles, including inflation and heavy taxation, eroded the loyalty of ordinary citizens. At the same time, the empire faced mounting external pressure from migrating peoples, who crossed the frontiers in increasing numbers and settled within imperial territory. The army, once Rome's greatest strength, became overstretched and increasingly reliant on foreign recruits.

Scholars continue to debate the relative importance of these factors. Some emphasize the role of invasions, while others stress the slow decay of civic institutions. What is clear is that the fall was not a sudden catastrophe but a long process of transformation, out of which the medieval societies of Europe eventually emerged.

toefl-r07.title: The Silk Road
toefl-r07.text:
The Silk Road was not a single road but a network of trade routes that connected East Asia with the Mediterranean world for more than a thousand years. Its name comes from silk, one of the most valuable goods carried along its length, yet the route also transported spices, precious metals, glass, and ideas. Merchants rarely traveled the entire distance; instead, goods passed through a chain of middlemen, changing hands many times before reaching their final destination.

The route flourished because powerful empires, such as those of China and Persia, provided the stability and security that long-distance trade required. Caravans of camels crossed deserts and mountains, stopping at oasis towns that grew into prosperous centers of commerce. These towns became melting pots where merchants, pilgrims, and scholars from different cultures met and exchanged knowledge.

The significance of the Silk Road extended far beyond economics. Religions such as Buddhism and Islam spread along its paths, and technologies including papermaking moved westward. When maritime trade routes became cheaper and more efficient in the early modern period, overland trade declined, but the cultural and commercial links the Silk Road had created endured.

toefl-r08.title: The Industrial Revolution
toefl-r08.text:
The Industrial Revolution, which began in Britain in the late eighteenth century, transformed the way goods were produced and, with it, the structure of society. Before this period, most people lived in the countryside and manufactured items by hand in their own homes. The introduction of machinery, powered first by water and later by steam, allowed production to be concentrated in factories, where output rose dramatically.

Several factors explain why Britain led the way. The country possessed abundant coal and iron, the raw materials that industry required. Its growing overseas empire provided both raw materials and markets for finished goods. A stable political system and a legal framework that protected property encouraged investment. Finally, a series of inventions, including the steam engine and the spinning jenny, steadily increased the efficiency of production.

The consequences were profound and far-reaching. Cities grew rapidly as workers left the countryside for factory jobs, and new social classes emerged. Working conditions in the early factories were often harsh, sparking movements for reform. Over time, industrialization spread to continental Europe and North America, reshaping economies and daily life around the globe.

toefl-r09.title: The Printing Press
toefl-r09.text:
The invention of the printing press in the mid-fifteenth century is widely regarded as one of the most important events in human history. Before its arrival, books had to be copied by hand, a slow and expensive process that made written knowledge the privilege of a small elite. Johannes Gutenberg's development of movable type changed this situation by making it possible to produce identical copies of a text quickly and cheaply.

The effects were dramatic. Books became affordable to a much wider audience, and literacy rates began to climb. Ideas could now travel across Europe with unprecedented speed, and scholars could compare and correct texts far more easily. The printing press played a central role in the religious upheavals of the Reformation, as reformers used it to spread their arguments, and in the Scientific Revolution, which depended on the rapid sharing of discoveries.

Historians often compare the printing press to the internet, since both technologies dramatically lowered the cost of distributing information. Each transformed the way people learn, argue, and organize their societies. The press did not merely reproduce books; it multiplied the power of ideas themselves.

toefl-r10.title: The Renaissance
toefl-r10.text:
The Renaissance, meaning rebirth, was a period of remarkable cultural achievement that began in Italy in the fourteenth century and spread across Europe. It represented a revival of interest in the literature, art, and learning of ancient Greece and Rome, which had been largely neglected during the Middle Ages. Scholars known as humanists turned to classical texts, seeking wisdom not only about the divine but also about human life and potential.

The movement was nourished by the prosperity of Italian city-states such as Florence and Venice, whose wealthy merchants and bankers patronized artists and thinkers. This patronage allowed figures like Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo to pursue ambitious projects. At the same time, the invention of the printing press enabled new ideas to circulate widely, accelerating the spread of Renaissance thought.

The Renaissance produced lasting changes in outlook. Artists developed techniques such as linear perspective that gave their work a new realism, while writers celebrated individual achievement and the dignity of the human spirit. This emphasis on the individual, along with a renewed confidence in reason and observation, helped set the stage for the scientific and social transformations of the modern era.

toefl-r11.title: Coral Reefs
toefl-r11.text:
Coral reefs are among the most productive and biologically diverse ecosystems on the planet. Although they cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, they provide habitat for roughly a quarter of all marine species. Reefs are built by tiny animals called coral polyps, which secrete hard skeletons of calcium carbonate. Over thousands of years, countless generations of these organisms construct the massive structures that we call reefs.

Reefs depend on a remarkable partnership. Within the tissues of the polyps live microscopic algae that use sunlight to produce food through photosynthesis, sharing much of it with their coral hosts. In return, the coral provides the algae with shelter and the compounds they need. Because the algae require sunlight, reefs grow only in clear, shallow, warm waters, which is why they are found mainly in tropical regions.

Today coral reefs face serious threats. Rising ocean temperatures can cause corals to expel their algae in a process called bleaching, which leaves the reefs white and weakened. Pollution, overfishing, and ocean acidification add further stress. Because reefs protect coastlines from storms and support the livelihoods of millions of people, their decline has consequences that reach far beyond the ocean itself.

toefl-r12.title: The Carbon Cycle
toefl-r12.text:
The carbon cycle describes how carbon, an element essential to all living things, moves through the atmosphere, oceans, land, and living organisms of Earth. Carbon exists in many forms, from the carbon dioxide gas in the air to the organic compounds that make up the bodies of plants and animals. The cycle keeps these different reservoirs in a rough balance, a balance that is vital to the stability of the climate of the planet.

Photosynthesis and respiration lie at the heart of the cycle. Plants absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and convert it into organic matter, which is then passed along the food chain. When organisms respire, or when dead material decays, carbon dioxide is released back into the atmosphere. Over much longer timescales, the burial of organic matter forms fossil fuels, while the weathering of rocks slowly removes carbon from the atmosphere.

Human activity has dramatically altered this cycle. The burning of fossil fuels releases carbon that had been locked underground for millions of years, raising the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Because carbon dioxide traps heat, this increase is the principal driver of modern climate change, making the carbon cycle one of the most closely studied processes in science.

toefl-r13.title: Migration
toefl-r13.text:
Migration is the regular, often seasonal movement of animals from one region to another, and it is among the most extraordinary phenomena in the natural world. Birds, fish, mammals, and even insects undertake journeys that can span thousands of miles. Arctic terns, for example, travel from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back each year, a round trip of tens of thousands of miles that allows them to experience nearly continuous daylight.

Animals migrate for a variety of reasons, but the search for food and suitable breeding conditions lies behind most journeys. Many species move to take advantage of abundant resources that appear only during certain seasons. Others travel to reach safe places where they can raise their young with fewer predators. The costs of migration are high: animals must store energy, navigate unfamiliar terrain, and survive storms and exhaustion along the way.

How migrating animals find their way remains a subject of intense study. Scientists have shown that some species use the position of the Sun and stars, while others sense the magnetic field of Earth or follow coastlines and mountain ranges. Recent research suggests that many migrants combine several of these cues, creating a navigation system more flexible and reliable than any single method alone.

toefl-r14.title: Rainforests
toefl-r14.text:
Tropical rainforests are the richest terrestrial ecosystems on Earth, home to an astonishing share of the species of the planet. Although they occupy only about six percent of the land surface, they are estimated to contain more than half of the plant and animal species of the world. This extraordinary diversity arises from the warm, wet, and stable climate of the tropics, which allows life to flourish year-round.

Rainforests are arranged in layers. The tallest trees form a dense canopy that absorbs most of the sunlight, while a middle layer of shorter trees and an understory of shrubs occupy the levels below. The forest floor remains dark and relatively open. Many animals are adapted to life in a single layer, and the competition for light, food, and space is intense, driving the evolution of countless specialized forms.

These forests also play a vital role in the health of the whole planet. Through photosynthesis, they absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen, and they regulate the flow of water through the atmosphere. Yet deforestation, driven by logging, agriculture, and mining, continues to destroy vast areas each year. The loss of rainforests threatens not only the species that live there but also the global climate systems on which humanity depends.

toefl-r15.title: Biodiversity and Extinction
toefl-r15.text:
Biodiversity, the variety of life in a particular habitat or across the planet as a whole, is essential to the functioning of ecosystems. Each species plays a role in the web of life, whether as a pollinator, a predator, a decomposer, or a source of food. Rich ecosystems tend to be more resilient: when one species declines, others can often compensate, allowing the system to recover from disturbance.

Yet extinction is a natural part of the history of Earth. In the background, species disappear at a slow, steady rate, and new ones evolve to take their place. At least five times in the deep past, however, catastrophic events wiped out large fractions of life in geologically short periods. The most famous of these mass extinctions eliminated the dinosaurs about sixty-six million years ago.

Many scientists now argue that we are entering a sixth mass extinction, this time caused by human activity. Habitat destruction, pollution, overexploitation, and climate change are driving species to disappear at rates far above the natural background. Because each loss weakens the intricate connections that sustain ecosystems, the erosion of biodiversity is considered one of the most urgent environmental challenges of our time.

toefl-r16.title: Artificial Intelligence
toefl-r16.text:
Artificial intelligence, or AI, refers to computer systems designed to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as recognizing speech, making decisions, and translating languages. The field emerged in the mid-twentieth century, when researchers first began to ask whether machines could be made to think. Early progress was slow, but steady advances in computing power and the availability of vast amounts of data have produced rapid breakthroughs in recent decades.

Modern AI relies heavily on a technique called machine learning, in which systems improve their performance by analyzing examples rather than following explicit instructions. A program might be shown millions of labeled images until it can identify objects on its own. This approach has led to systems that can play complex games, drive cars, and assist in medical diagnosis. At the same time, the technology raises difficult questions about privacy, bias, and the future of work.

As AI becomes woven into daily life, experts debate both its promise and its risks. Proponents emphasize gains in efficiency and new capabilities, while critics warn of unintended consequences. What is clear is that AI will continue to reshape society, making informed public discussion of its development more important than ever.

toefl-r17.title: The Internet
toefl-r17.text:
The internet is a global network that connects billions of computers, allowing them to exchange information almost instantly. Its origins lie in research projects of the 1960s, when scientists sought a way to link computers across great distances and to keep communications functioning even if parts of the network failed. What began as a tool for researchers and the military has grown into a system that touches nearly every aspect of modern life.

The internet works by breaking information into small packets of data, which travel independently through the network and are reassembled at their destination. Because there is no single central authority controlling the system, it is remarkably robust: if one path is blocked, the packets can simply find another. This design, known as packet switching, was a key innovation that made the network flexible and resilient.

The social and economic effects of the internet have been enormous. It has transformed commerce, education, and communication, creating new industries and new ways of working. At the same time, it has raised concerns about privacy, security, and the spread of misinformation. As the network continues to evolve, balancing its benefits against its risks remains a central challenge for society.

toefl-r18.title: Renewable Energy
toefl-r18.text:
Renewable energy comes from sources that are naturally replenished, such as sunlight, wind, moving water, and the heat of Earth. Unlike fossil fuels, which exist in limited quantities and release carbon dioxide when burned, these sources are continuously available and produce little or no pollution. For this reason, they are central to efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and slow climate change.

The most widely used renewable technologies include solar panels, which convert sunlight directly into electricity, and wind turbines, which harness the movement of the air. Hydroelectric dams generate power from falling water, while geothermal plants tap heat stored beneath the surface of Earth. Each technology has advantages and limitations: solar and wind power, for example, are intermittent, since the Sun does not always shine and the wind does not always blow.

The transition to renewable energy presents considerable challenges. Storage systems are needed to hold energy for times when generation is low, and existing electrical grids must be modernized to carry power from remote sites to cities. Nevertheless, the cost of renewables has fallen sharply in recent years, and they now compete with traditional fuels in many markets, suggesting that the clean-energy transition is well under way.

toefl-r19.title: Space Exploration
toefl-r19.text:
Space exploration, the investigation of the universe beyond the atmosphere of Earth, has transformed our understanding of the cosmos and our place within it. Beginning with the launch of the first artificial satellites in the 1950s, humans have sent probes to every planet in the solar system, landed on the Moon, and placed powerful telescopes in orbit. These missions have revealed worlds of astonishing variety, from the volcanoes of Venus to the ice-covered oceans of the moon Europa.

The pursuit of space exploration has produced practical benefits as well as scientific knowledge. Technologies developed for space missions have found uses on Earth in fields as diverse as medicine, communications, and weather forecasting. Satellites monitor the climate of the planet, guide navigation systems, and connect remote regions to global networks. At the same time, exploration satisfies a deeper human desire to understand the unknown.

The future of space exploration is uncertain but full of possibility. Plans for returning to the Moon and eventually reaching Mars raise difficult questions about cost, risk, and international cooperation. Whether pursued by governments or private companies, the endeavor continues to inspire new generations of scientists and engineers, and it remains one of the great collective undertakings of the human species.

toefl-r20.title: Cryptography
toefl-r20.text:
Cryptography is the science of securing information by transforming it into a form that only authorized parties can read. Its history stretches back thousands of years, to the simple substitution ciphers used by ancient rulers to protect military and diplomatic messages. In such systems, each letter of a message is replaced by another according to a secret rule, so that an intercepted message appears to be nonsense to anyone who lacks the key.

Modern cryptography is vastly more sophisticated. Because computers can perform calculations at extraordinary speed, old codes that once seemed secure can now be broken in moments. In response, mathematicians have developed techniques based on difficult problems, such as factoring very large numbers, that even powerful computers cannot solve quickly. These methods secure the transactions that underlie online banking, e-commerce, and private communication.

Cryptography also protects more than money and messages. It underpins the authentication systems that verify identity and the digital signatures that guarantee a document has not been altered. As more of daily life moves online, the discipline has become essential to trust in the digital world. Researchers continue to prepare for the arrival of quantum computers, which may one day break many of the methods in use today.

toefl-r21.title: Memory
toefl-r21.text:
Memory is the process by which the mind encodes, stores, and retrieves information, and it is fundamental to nearly everything we do. Psychologists often divide memory into several types. Sensory memory holds fleeting impressions of what we see and hear for a fraction of a second, while short-term memory keeps a small amount of information available for a brief period, such as a phone number we repeat to ourselves. Long-term memory, by contrast, can store vast quantities of information for years.

One of the most important discoveries in the study of memory is that remembering is not a passive playback of events. Instead, it is an active process of reconstruction, in which the brain fills gaps using expectations and prior knowledge. This helps explain why two people can remember the same event differently, and why memories can be distorted over time or even implanted by suggestion. Such findings have had serious consequences for the reliability of eyewitness testimony in court.

Researchers have also shown that memory can be improved through strategies such as organizing information, spacing study sessions, and linking new material to what is already known. Understanding how memory works, and how it fails, continues to shape both education and the legal system.

toefl-r22.title: The Nature of Dreams
toefl-r22.text:
For much of human history, dreams were regarded as messages from the gods or glimpses of the future. Modern psychology offers very different explanations. Sigmund Freud, the founder of psychoanalysis, proposed that dreams are the disguised expression of repressed wishes, a safety valve through which forbidden desires find symbolic release. While few researchers accept the theory of Freud in full, his work established dreaming as a serious subject of scientific study.

A more recent and influential account is the activation-synthesis hypothesis. According to this view, dreams are the attempt of the brain to make sense of random bursts of neural activity that occur during rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep. The brain, deprived of external input, weaves these signals into a story, however strange or illogical it may seem. This explains the bizarre quality of many dreams, in which familiar places and people appear in impossible combinations.

Other researchers suggest that dreaming serves important functions, such as consolidating memories and rehearsing responses to threatening situations. Although scientists still disagree about why we dream, there is broad consensus that dreaming is closely tied to the activity of the brain during sleep and that it plays a role in emotional and cognitive health.

toefl-r23.title: The Bystander Effect
toefl-r23.text:
The bystander effect is a well-documented phenomenon in social psychology: the more people who witness an emergency, the less likely any single individual is to offer help. This counterintuitive finding emerged from research following the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese, a case in which numerous neighbors reportedly heard her cries yet no one intervened. Psychologists wondered how so many people could remain passive.

Experiments by John Darley and Bibb Latane revealed part of the answer. When participants believed they were the only witness to a crisis, most acted quickly to help. But when they believed others were also present, the rate of helping dropped sharply. The researchers identified two key processes. One is diffusion of responsibility, the feeling that someone else will surely take action. The other is pluralistic ignorance, in which people look to others for cues and, seeing no one react, conclude that no emergency exists.

The bystander effect has important practical implications. Training programs now encourage people to single out an individual and ask for help directly, and to recognize the social forces that can inhibit action. Understanding why good people sometimes fail to act is a first step toward overcoming that failure.

toefl-r24.title: Cognitive Biases
toefl-r24.text:
Human beings like to think of themselves as rational, but decades of research in psychology have shown that our judgments are shaped by systematic errors known as cognitive biases. These are mental shortcuts, or heuristics, that usually serve us well but sometimes lead us astray. Understanding them has become central to fields ranging from economics to medicine.

One of the best known is confirmation bias, the tendency to seek out and remember information that supports our existing beliefs while ignoring evidence that contradicts them. This bias helps explain why people with opposing views often reach opposite conclusions from the same facts. Another is the availability heuristic, in which we judge how common or likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Dramatic events, such as plane crashes, are easy to recall, so people tend to overestimate their frequency while underestimating more ordinary risks.

Researchers stress that biases are not signs of stupidity; they affect experts and laypeople alike. The first step in counteracting them is awareness. By slowing down, seeking diverse sources of information, and considering alternative explanations, people can reduce the influence of bias on their decisions, though the biases themselves can never be entirely eliminated.

toefl-r25.title: The Development of Language
toefl-r25.text:
How children acquire language so rapidly is one of the great questions of cognitive science. By the age of three or four, most children can produce and understand sentences they have never heard before, a remarkable feat that no computer program has fully matched. Researchers generally agree that language learning depends on both innate abilities and experience, but they disagree sharply about the relative importance of each.

The linguist Noam Chomsky argued that children are born with an innate capacity for grammar, a built-in knowledge of the underlying principles shared by all human languages. This, he claimed, explains why children everywhere master their native tongue on roughly the same schedule, despite enormous differences in their environments. Critics, however, point out that children learn an enormous amount through interaction, imitation, and feedback from caregivers, and that statistical patterns in the speech they hear provide rich information.

Most researchers now favor a middle position. Children seem to come into the world equipped with powerful general learning mechanisms and a strong social drive, which together allow them to crack the code of language with astonishing speed. The study of language acquisition continues to illuminate the relationship between nature and nurture in human development.

toefl-r26.title: The History of Photography
toefl-r26.text:
Photography, the art and science of creating images by recording light, transformed the way people see and remember the world. The first permanent photograph was produced in the 1820s, and by the middle of the nineteenth century techniques such as the daguerreotype made portrait photography widely available. For the first time, ordinary people could possess accurate images of themselves and their families.

The new medium immediately raised questions about its relationship to art. Some painters feared that photography would make their craft obsolete, since a camera could capture a scene far more quickly and accurately than a brush. Others embraced the technology, using photographs as aids for composition and study. Over time, photographers themselves began to argue that their work deserved recognition as art, composing their images with the same care as any painter.

The twentieth century brought further revolutions. Lightweight cameras allowed photographers to work in the street and on the battlefield, and the rise of photojournalism gave the medium a powerful role in shaping public opinion. Today, digital technology has made photography nearly universal, but debates about authenticity, manipulation, and the boundary between record and art continue to animate the field.

toefl-r27.title: The Novel
toefl-r27.text:
The novel, a long work of prose fiction, is one of the most popular and influential literary forms ever created. Although stories of adventure and romance are ancient, the novel as we know it emerged in Europe in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, when rising literacy and the spread of printing created a new reading public. Writers such as Daniel Defoe and Samuel Richardson helped establish a form that focused on the inner lives of ordinary people.

The great advantage of the novel is its capacity to explore character in depth. Unlike drama, which must compress a story into a few hours of performance, the novel can unfold gradually, following individuals across years and allowing readers to enter their thoughts. This made the novel an ideal vehicle for examining the moral and social questions of its age, from the position of women to the effects of industrial change.

The form has proved extraordinarily adaptable. In the nineteenth century, novelists such as Dickens and Tolstoy used it to paint vast portraits of society, while modern writers have experimented with structure, voice, and time. Even as new media have arisen, the novel has persisted, continually renewing itself and remaining central to how we understand human experience.

toefl-r28.title: Impressionism
toefl-r28.text:
Impressionism was an artistic movement that emerged in France in the 1870s and revolutionized Western painting. Its leading figures, including Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, broke with the conventions of the official art world, which favored carefully finished canvases depicting historical and mythological subjects. The Impressionists instead painted everyday scenes, and they sought to capture the fleeting effects of light and atmosphere rather than precise detail.

The name of the movement came from a scornful review of a Monet painting titled Impression, Sunrise. The artists adopted the label defiantly. Working outdoors, often directly in front of their subjects, they applied paint in short, visible strokes of bright color, allowing the eye of the viewer to blend the colors at a distance. This technique was ideally suited to conveying shimmering water, moving crowds, and the shifting quality of daylight.

At first the public and critics reacted with hostility, and the Impressionists struggled to sell their work. Within a few decades, however, their approach had won acceptance and transformed the course of art. By liberating painters from the demand for photographic accuracy, Impressionism opened the door to the many movements of modern art that followed.

toefl-r29.title: Architecture
toefl-r29.text:
Architecture is the art and science of designing buildings, and it reflects the values, technology, and aspirations of the societies that produce it. From the temples of ancient Greece to the skyscrapers of the modern city, buildings have always served purposes that go far beyond shelter. They express power, embody religious belief, and shape the daily experience of the people who use them.

Throughout history, architecture has evolved in response to changes in materials and engineering. The invention of concrete allowed the Romans to construct vast domes and arches, while the development of steel frames in the nineteenth century made it possible to build upward, giving rise to the skyscraper. Each innovation expanded what architects could imagine and achieve, and each generation reinterpreted older styles to suit new needs.

Architecture also has profound social consequences. The design of the buildings and public spaces of a city influences how people move, interact, and feel. Crowded, poorly lit housing can harm health and morale, while well-designed spaces can foster community and well-being.
