Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide trap heat in the atmosphere that would otherwise escape into space, and since the industrial revolution their concentration has risen to levels not seen for hundreds of thousands of years. The consequences are already visible in rising sea levels, retreating glaciers, more intense heat waves, and shifts in the ranges of plants and animals. Climate models, which simulate the behavior of the atmosphere and oceans, project that these changes will accelerate unless emissions are reduced sharply.

The central challenge of addressing climate change is not scientific but political and economic. The benefits of reducing emissions are global and long-term, while the costs of action are borne in the present and concentrated on particular industries and regions. This mismatch explains why coordinated action has been so difficult to achieve, despite decades of international negotiations. Proposed solutions include shifting to renewable energy, improving efficiency, and removing carbon from the atmosphere. Many economists favor putting a price on carbon, so that polluters face the true cost of their emissions. The scale of the problem is immense, but the technologies needed to address it exist; what has been missing is the collective will to deploy them at the required speed.

yokdil-r27.title: The Loss of Biodiversity
yokdil-r27.text:
Biodiversity, the variety of life on Earth, is declining at a rate that many scientists describe as the sixth mass extinction in the planet's history. Unlike earlier mass extinctions, which were caused by natural events such as asteroid impacts or volcanic eruptions, the current crisis is driven almost entirely by human activity. The destruction of natural habitats for agriculture, urban expansion, and resource extraction is the leading cause, but overexploitation, pollution, the spread of invasive species, and climate change all contribute. Species are now disappearing at a rate hundreds or even thousands of times higher than the natural background rate.

The loss of biodiversity matters for reasons that extend far beyond the value of any individual species. Ecosystems provide services that human societies depend on, including the purification of water, the pollination of crops, the control of pests, and the regulation of climate. When the web of life is simplified, these services become less reliable and more expensive to replace. Moreover, biodiversity represents a vast library of genetic and chemical information that has already yielded medicines, materials, and crop varieties. Its loss is therefore irreversible in practical terms, since evolution cannot recreate lost species on any human timescale. Protecting what remains, scientists argue, is not a luxury but a necessity for human well-being.

yokdil-r28.title: Plate Tectonics
yokdil-r28.text:
The theory of plate tectonics, developed in the 1960s, transformed geology by explaining how the surface of the Earth is organized and why it changes. According to the theory, the Earth's outer shell is divided into a number of rigid plates that float on the semi-fluid layer beneath and move slowly over geological time. Where plates pull apart, molten rock rises to form new crust, as along the mid-ocean ridges. Where they collide, one plate may slide beneath another, a process that builds mountain ranges and fuels the volcanoes and earthquakes that ring the Pacific Ocean. The theory provided a unifying explanation for phenomena that had long puzzled scientists, including the matching shapes of continents and the distribution of fossils.

The evidence for plate tectonics is extensive. The discovery that rocks on the ocean floor record a pattern of magnetic reversals, symmetrical on either side of the ridges, demonstrated that the seafloor is spreading. Satellite measurements now track plate motion in real time, confirming the slow drift, usually a few centimeters per year, that the theory predicts. Understanding plate motion has practical value as well, since it underpins efforts to assess the risks of earthquakes and volcanic eruptions and to locate resources such as minerals and oil. What once seemed a fixed and unchanging Earth is now understood as a dynamic system in constant, if gradual, motion.

yokdil-r29.title: The Strange World of Quantum Mechanics
yokdil-r29.text:
Quantum mechanics, developed in the early twentieth century, describes the behavior of matter and energy at the scale of atoms and subatomic particles, where the intuitive rules of everyday physics break down. One of its most striking features is that particles do not have definite positions until they are measured; instead, they are described by probabilities. Another is superposition, the ability of a quantum system to exist in multiple states at once, and its counterpart, entanglement, in which the properties of two particles become linked so that measuring one instantly determines the other, no matter how far apart they are. Albert Einstein famously found such features troubling, yet experiments have repeatedly confirmed their reality.

Quantum theory is far more than a philosophical curiosity. It underlies the technologies of the modern world, including the transistors that power computers and the lasers used in medicine and telecommunications. Today, researchers are exploiting the stranger aspects of quantum behavior to build new kinds of machines. Quantum computers, which process information using superposition and entanglement, could in principle solve certain problems far faster than any classical computer. Quantum cryptography promises communication that is secure against any eavesdropper. Although formidable engineering obstacles remain, the field has moved from abstract theory to a central driver of innovation.

yokdil-r30.title: Photosynthesis and Its Lessons
yokdil-r30.text:
Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae, and certain bacteria convert sunlight into chemical energy, and it is the foundation of nearly all life on Earth. Using light energy, these organisms combine carbon dioxide from the air with water to produce sugars, releasing oxygen as a byproduct. The sugars store the sun's energy in a form that living cells can use, and they are passed along the food chain to all other organisms, including humans. The oxygen produced by photosynthesis, accumulated over billions of years, transformed the Earth's atmosphere and made possible the evolution of complex animal life.

Scientists have long been interested in photosynthesis not only because of its biological importance but also because of its remarkable efficiency at capturing energy. Researchers study its molecular machinery, the protein complexes that harvest light and drive chemical reactions, hoping to learn lessons that could improve human technologies. Artificial photosynthesis, which aims to mimic the process to produce fuels from sunlight and water, offers the prospect of storing solar energy in a portable chemical form. Improving the efficiency of crop photosynthesis is another active area of research, since even modest gains could significantly increase food production. In this way, a process that evolved billions of years ago may hold the key to meeting some of the most pressing energy and food challenges of the future.

gre-r01.title: Scientific Revolutions and Paradigm Shifts
gre-r01.text:
The history of science is often told as a steady accumulation of facts, with each generation building patiently on the discoveries of the last. The historian Thomas Kuhn famously challenged this picture, arguing that science advances not by gradual accretion but by periodic upheavals he called paradigm shifts. A paradigm, in his usage, is the constellation of assumptions, methods and exemplary results that define normal science within a community at a given time.

According to Kuhn, scientists working within a paradigm rarely test or question its foundations; they solve puzzles according to its rules. But anomalies, observations that resist explanation, accumulate over time and eventually provoke a crisis. A new paradigm then emerges, often proposed by younger or marginal practitioners, and if it accounts for the anomalies more successfully, the community converts to it. Because the new paradigm rests on different assumptions, Kuhn argued, its adoption is not a purely logical process but involves persuasion and even something like conversion.

Kuhn's account provoked intense debate. His critics charged that he made science appear irrational, driven by fashion rather than evidence. His defenders replied that he described how science actually works, and that the willingness of scientists to abandon cherished frameworks in the face of evidence remains one of its greatest strengths.

gre-r02.title: Quantum Mechanics and Determinism
gre-r02.text:
For two centuries after Newton, physicists assumed that the universe was deterministic: given complete knowledge of the present, the entire future could in principle be predicted. The discovery of quantum mechanics in the early twentieth century shattered this assumption. At the level of atoms and particles, the theory describes probabilities rather than certainties, and it famously refuses to assign definite properties, such as position and momentum, to a particle before measurement.

Einstein, who contributed to the theory's foundations, never reconciled himself to its implications, declaring that God does not play dice. Niels Bohr, his principal antagonist, insisted that the probabilistic account was not a stopgap but the deepest possible description of nature. For decades the dispute remained philosophical, but experiments later confirmed one of the theory's most astonishing predictions, that measuring a particle can instantly affect the state of another particle far away, a phenomenon called entanglement, which Einstein dismissed as spooky action at a distance.

Quantum mechanics is now the most accurately tested theory in the history of science, and its practical fruits, from lasers to microchips, are everywhere. Yet the interpretation of what it tells us about reality remains unsettled, and the question of whether nature is fundamentally probabilistic or merely appears so continues to occupy physicists and philosophers alike.

gre-r03.title: The Expanding Universe
gre-r03.text:
Until the 1920s, most astronomers assumed that the universe was static and eternal, a fixed stage on which the stars played out their long histories. Edwin Hubble changed that view forever when he observed that distant galaxies are receding from us, and that the farther away a galaxy lies, the faster it moves. The most natural interpretation was that the universe itself is expanding, which in turn implied that it had a beginning, a moment of extraordinary density and heat now called the Big Bang.

This conclusion was deeply unwelcome to many scientists, and even Einstein had inserted a fudge factor into his equations to keep the universe stationary. Yet the evidence accumulated. The discovery of the cosmic microwave background radiation in 1965, a faint glow left over from the hot early phase, provided spectacular confirmation of the theory. Later observations showed that the expansion is not slowing down as gravity should dictate but accelerating, driven by a mysterious force dubbed dark energy whose nature remains one of the great unsolved problems of physics.

The Big Bang theory is not a story of creation in any religious sense; it describes the earliest moments from which the observable universe developed. What happened before that threshold, and whether the expansion will continue forever, are questions that lie beyond the reach of present observations and may always remain there.

gre-r04.title: Plate Tectonics and Continental Drift
gre-r04.text:
The theory of plate tectonics is to geology what evolution is to biology: a unifying idea that explains an enormous range of observations. According to the theory, the outer shell of the Earth is divided into a dozen or so rigid plates that float on the hotter, slowly churning mantle beneath. These plates move at rates of a few centimetres per year, and their boundaries are where the drama of the planet unfolds.

Where plates collide, one may plunge beneath the other, forming deep trenches and chains of volcanoes; where they separate, magma rises and new ocean floor is created. Where they slide past one another, they build up stress that is released in earthquakes, as along the San Andreas fault. The theory also explains the distribution of fossils and rock types across continents, which look as if they were torn apart from a single landmass that geologists call Pangaea.

Though the idea that continents drift was proposed early in the twentieth century by Alfred Wegener, it was dismissed for decades, in part because no convincing mechanism could be identified and in part because Wegener was not a geologist. The decisive evidence came after the Second World War from studies of the ocean floor and from the discovery of reversals in the Earth's magnetic field recorded in the rocks. Within a remarkably short time the scepticism collapsed, and plate tectonics became the accepted foundation of the Earth sciences.

gre-r05.title: Chaos Theory and Prediction
gre-r05.text:
Chaos theory studies systems that behave unpredictably despite being governed by perfectly deterministic laws. The classic example is the weather: in principle the atmosphere obeys the equations of physics, yet small differences in initial conditions grow so rapidly that reliable prediction beyond a week or two is impossible. This sensitivity to initial conditions is popularly known as the butterfly effect, the idea that the flap of a butterfly's wings in one place might ultimately contribute to a storm elsewhere.

The pioneers of chaos theory encountered this behaviour in the 1960s, when Edward Lorenz, a meteorologist, discovered that rounding a number in his weather model to three decimal places instead of six produced utterly different forecasts. At first he assumed an error; in time he understood that he had stumbled onto a deep property of nonlinear systems. Since then chaos has been found everywhere, in the orbits of planets, the rhythms of the heart, the fluctuations of markets and the growth of populations.

Chaos should not be confused with randomness. Chaotic systems are deterministic, meaning that given perfect information their futures are fixed, but their behaviour is so sensitive that perfect information is unattainable in practice. The practical consequence is a limit on prediction, and the philosophical consequence is a reminder that the world is more intricately structured than simple cause-and-effect stories suggest.

gre-r06.title: The Value of the Humanities
gre-r06.text:
The humanities, the disciplines that study what human beings have made, thought and felt, are under siege. Funding is being cut, departments merged or closed, and students increasingly steered toward subjects that promise immediate employment. In the prevailing language of policy, the value of a course of study is measured by graduate salaries, and by that measure the humanities fare poorly.

Yet the case for them is not merely nostalgic. The humanities train precisely the capacities that a technology-driven economy claims to prize: the ability to read closely and think critically, to weigh evidence and construct arguments, to understand perspectives unlike one's own and to communicate with precision. Employers consistently report that such skills are scarce, and historians of innovation argue that creativity flourishes where technical competence is joined to broad knowledge and historical awareness.

Defenders of the humanities are sometimes accused of defending privilege or resisting change. But the strongest defence is practical as much as cultural. A society that understands only how to make things, and not how to ask what things are for, is impoverished in ways that no spreadsheet can measure. The question is not whether the humanities deserve to survive but whether a civilisation can afford to neglect them.

gre-r07.title: Translation and Cultural Exchange
gre-r07.text:
Every translation is a small act of betrayal, or so translators like to joke, because no two languages carve the world up in the same way. German can say Gedankenexperiment in a word, Italian uses a whole sentence, and English must split a thought that Russian keeps whole. The translator must choose, and every choice loses something, a connotation, a rhythm, an ambiguity the author cultivated deliberately. This is why the Italian proverb warns that to translate is to betray.

The impossibility of perfect equivalence has not, however, stopped translation, because the alternative is silence. The great translation projects of history, from the rendering of Greek philosophy into Arabic and Latin to the modern mass translation of world literature, have been engines of cultural renewal. When knowledge crosses a linguistic border, it is not simply copied but transformed, and the transformation often produces something new, as when the Bible translated into vernacular languages reshaped the cultures that read it.

Debates about literal and free translation have raged for two thousand years, and they will never be settled, because the right answer depends on purpose. A contract should be translated literally, a poem freely, and the best translators move between the poles, preserving what matters most for their audience. In this sense translation is less a science than a practiced art, and its history is the history of how ideas travel and change.

gre-r08.title: The Epic Tradition
gre-r08.text:
The epic is the oldest literary form still practised, and it has never lost its hold on the imagination. Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, composed nearly three thousand years ago, established the pattern: a hero of superhuman prowess, a vast setting, warfare and wandering, and the constant intervention of gods in human affairs. Yet what made the epics great was not spectacle but what later critics called the tragic questions, the ways in which they probe honour, mortality, rage and the cost of greatness.

The epic form has proved remarkably adaptable. Virgil's Aeneid turned Greek models to Roman purposes, presenting Aeneas as the founder of a people and, some say, a justification for empire. Dante made his Divine Comedy, a journey through the afterlife, in vernacular Italian rather than Latin, and in doing so helped create a language's literary identity. Milton's Paradise Lost retold the fall of humanity in a Protestant epic that measured itself against the ancients, and modern poets and novelists, from Joyce to Walcott, have continued to mine the form.

Critics have argued that the epic belongs to an age of war and heroes that has passed. Others reply that the form survives not because it celebrates violence but because it asks the largest questions a culture can ask about what it means to be human, questions that do not date. As long as those questions remain unanswered, the epic, in some new guise, will find its poets.

gre-r09.title: The Problem of Consciousness
gre-r09.text:
How does a lump of matter in the skull produce thoughts, feelings and the vivid inner life each of us knows directly? The problem of consciousness is sometimes called the last great mystery of science, and it has occupied philosophers since Descartes, who divided the world into extended matter and thinking mind, a division that made the connection between the two all but inexplicable. Since his time the question has only deepened as neuroscience has shown in exquisite detail how mental life depends on brain activity.

One influential answer, physicalism, holds that consciousness is nothing over and above brain processes, that experience just is a certain kind of neural activity. The difficulty, as critics point out, is that no account of neurons seems to capture what it is like to taste coffee or feel pain, the qualitative character that philosophers call qualia. Other thinkers propose that consciousness is an illusion of sorts, or that it emerges from complexity in ways we cannot yet follow, or even that it may be a fundamental feature of reality, as basic as space and time.

The stakes are practical as well as theoretical. If machine intelligence ever approaches human levels, the question of whether machines could be conscious will force decisions in ethics and law for which no precedent exists. Whatever the answer, consciousness is the one aspect of the universe we know from the inside, and understanding it may require new concepts rather than simply more data.

gre-r10.title: The Rise of the Novel
gre-r10.text:
The novel is a surprisingly recent invention. While poetry and drama reach back to antiquity, the novel as we know it, a long prose fiction about the ordinary lives of recognisable people, took shape in Europe in the eighteenth century. Early works such as Defoe's Robinson Crusoe and Richardson's Pamela presented themselves as true histories, and this claim to realism, the sense that the story could have happened to the reader, was precisely what made the form new.

Its rise is linked to deep social changes. The growth of the reading public, the expansion of literacy, the arrival of circulating libraries and the leisure of a rising middle class created an audience eager for stories about courtship, money and social ascent. The novel was the first literary form to be consumed by women in large numbers, and its great practitioners, from Fielding to Austen, made an art of domestic life and the private moral drama of choice.

Critics sometimes dismiss the novel as mere entertainment, but its history suggests otherwise. Because it could represent whole societies in unprecedented detail, the novel became a privileged instrument of social criticism, exposing hypocrisy and injustice, and a laboratory for exploring the inner life, the stream of consciousness that later writers would push to its limits. More than two centuries on, it remains the form best suited to answering that question no other art asks so persistently: how do we live with one another?

gre-r11.title: The Economics of Inequality
gre-r11.text:
Inequality of income and wealth has risen sharply in most advanced economies since around 1980, a reversal of the long convergence that followed the Second World War. The causes are debated. Many economists point to technology, which rewards high-skilled workers with a premium while automating routine jobs; others point to globalisation, deregulation, declining union membership and changes in taxation that favour capital over labour.

What is less often disputed is the consequence. Research suggests that high inequality is associated with lower social mobility, weaker health outcomes and, beyond a point, slower growth, as the wealthy save rather than spend and the rest are left with too little to invest in education or enterprise. Political scientists add a further cost: when the gap widens, trust in institutions erodes and politics polarises, as citizens conclude that the game is rigged against them.

There is no consensus on the remedy. Some favour higher marginal taxes and stronger social spending; others argue that growth itself is the cure and that redistribution crushes the incentives that create wealth. What both sides concede is that the present trajectory is not sustainable, and that the question of how much inequality a democracy can tolerate will define the political economy of the coming decades.

gre-r12.title: Behavioural Economics and Rationality
gre-r12.text:
Classical economics assumed that people act rationally, weighing costs and benefits and choosing what serves their interests. Over the past half century this assumption has been dismantled, most influentially by the psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, whose research showed that human judgment is riddled with systematic errors. Far from random, these biases are predictable, and they shape everything from retirement saving to the choice of a mortgage.

Among the best documented is loss aversion: losses hurt roughly twice as much as equivalent gains please, which helps explain why investors hold losing stocks too long and why people pay heavily for insurance. Present bias, the tendency to discount the future so steeply that tomorrow never quite arrives, undermines saving and healthy eating. Anchoring shows that an arbitrary starting number, such as a suggested retail price, can pull final judgments toward itself. Taken together, such findings suggest that the rational actor of classical theory is a fiction, though a useful one.

The practical outgrowth of this research is nudging, the design of choices so that the effortless option is the wise one. Making pension enrolment automatic, so that people must act to opt out, raised participation dramatically. Critics object that nudging manipulates people, but its defenders reply that choices must be framed somehow, and that helping people choose better without forbidding anything is a modest and honest art.

gre-r13.title: The Gig Economy
gre-r13.text:
The gig economy promises flexibility. Its advocates describe a world in which workers choose when and how much to work, fitting tasks around family and study, using platforms and apps to find customers and keep every minute productive. For students, carers and others who cannot commit to a fixed schedule, the promise is real.

But critics argue that flexibility is often one-sided. Platforms that connect drivers, couriers and freelance workers classify many of them as independent contractors rather than employees, which relieves companies of obligations such as minimum wage, paid leave, health insurance and unemployment protection. The worker bears the risks, the costs of vehicle and equipment, and the silence of idle hours, while the platform profits from every transaction. Income is unpredictable, protections are thin, and the algorithm that assigns work is a black box that can suddenly exclude a worker with no appeal.

Regulation has struggled to keep pace. Courts in several countries have ruled that some gig workers should be treated as employees, and new laws have sought to guarantee minimum earnings and benefits while preserving genuine flexibility. The deeper question is whether the gains in convenience and autonomy can be combined with security, or whether the gig economy represents a permanent erosion of the protections that a century of labour law built. The answer will determine what work means for a generation.

gre-r14.title: Urbanization and the Megacity
gre-r14.text:
For the first time in human history, more people live in cities than in the countryside, and the world's urban population is still growing by roughly two hundred thousand people a day. The megacity, an urban region of ten million or more, has become a signature of the era: Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai and their counterparts absorb migrants drawn by jobs, education and the sheer density of opportunity that only cities offer.

The urban turn has brought historic gains. Cities concentrate talent and ideas, and economists have shown that productivity rises with density, as people exchange skills, spark firms and shorten the distance between a thought and a market. For the rural poor, the move to the city, even to an informal settlement, has often meant better access to services and a step up the income ladder.

The costs, however, are also concentrated. Housing prices in successful cities exclude the young, and the poor often live in sprawling, underserviced peripheries far from jobs. Congestion, pollution and the emissions of urban life strain health and climate. Yet the pessimism of an earlier generation, which predicted that cities would collapse under their own weight, has proved unfounded; cities are difficult, expensive and inefficient in many ways, but they also work, and the world shows no sign of wanting to live any other way.

gre-r15.title: The Sociology of Social Networks
gre-r15.text:
A social network is more than the sum of its members, as the sociologists who pioneered the field demonstrated long before the internet made the term a household word. By mapping who is connected to whom, researchers found that position in a network shapes outcomes: those with many connections enjoy advantages in finding jobs, spreading ideas and gaining influence, while those at the margins are often last to learn what is happening.

The most famous demonstration is the small world experiment, in which letters passed from stranger to stranger reached a distant target in only about six steps, a finding popularised as six degrees of separation. Later work refined the picture: it is not mere connection that matters but the structure of the network, its clusters, bridges and hub nodes, that determines how quickly information flows and how robust the whole system is to the removal of key individuals.

Social networks also transmit more than information; they transmit behaviour. Smoking, obesity and happiness have all been shown to spread through ties of friendship, a finding that complicates the simple story of personal choice. The practical lesson is that intervening in a network, by targeting its hubs or closing its bridges, can change outcomes for thousands of people who were never directly addressed. Networks, in short, do not just describe society; they shape it.

gre-r16.title: Evolution by Natural Selection
gre-r16.text:
The theory of evolution by natural selection, proposed jointly by Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace in 1858, is the organising principle of biology. Its logic is disarmingly simple. Individuals vary; more offspring are produced than can survive; the variants best suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce; and because these variants are heritable, they accumulate over generations. Given enough time, small differences compound into new species, and all the diversity of life follows from a single common ancestor.

The evidence is now overwhelming and comes from every direction: the fossil record, which shows orderly change through time; comparative anatomy, in which the same bones are recognisably rearranged across species; and molecular biology, which reads the same history in the sequences of DNA shared by all organisms. Biologists speak of evolution not as a hypothesis but as a fact, in the same sense that the roundness of the Earth is a fact.

This does not mean the theory is finished. Natural selection explains adaptation, but much else, the origin of life, the evolution of consciousness, the details of how variation is generated, remains under active investigation. Yet the modern debates concern the how, not the whether. Since Darwin, no serious alternative has survived contact with the evidence, and the theory's power to explain disparate facts is precisely what makes it scientific.

gre-r17.title: Epigenetics and Gene Activity
gre-r17.text:
Your genome, the sequence of DNA inherited from your parents, is fixed at conception, yet the way your body uses it is not. Epigenetics, the study of heritable changes in gene activity that do not involve changes to the DNA sequence itself, has revealed that the genome reads as much like sheet music as like a fixed blueprint. Chemical tags attached to DNA and to the proteins around it switch genes on and off in response to the environment and the experiences of the organism.

The scope of the finding is startling. Studies with animals show that diet, stress and even the care received early in life can leave marks that alter behaviour and health, and some of these marks appear to be transmitted to offspring, a suggestion that parents may pass on not only genes but a kind of environmental memory. Researchers caution that such transgenerational inheritance in humans remains controversial and that most differences between people are still explained by the genome itself.

What epigenetics has decisively changed is the scientific mood. The old opposition between nature and nurture has collapsed, because the two are now seen to interact at the molecular level: experience gets written into the biology of the organism. The hope is that epigenetic knowledge will lead to therapies that reverse harmful marks, and the warning embedded in the same knowledge is that early environments may matter more, and last longer, than was ever supposed.

gre-r18.title: The Human Microbiome
gre-r18.text:
The human body is home to trillions of microorganisms, chiefly bacteria, that outnumber human cells and carry far more genes than the human genome itself. This community, the microbiome, was once treated as an infection to be minimised, but research over the past two decades has reversed that view: the microbes that inhabit the gut, skin and mouth are now understood as partners in health, aiding digestion, synthesising vitamins and training the immune system.

The connections are astonishingly broad. Differences in gut bacteria have been linked to obesity, diabetes, allergies and even mood and behaviour, through pathways that scientists describe with the evocative phrase gut-brain axis. Antibiotics, while essential, disrupt the community, and evidence suggests that repeated courses in childhood may have long-term effects that were never anticipated. The rise of caesarean births, which bypass the exposure to maternal bacteria that accompanies vaginal delivery, has prompted questions about the development of the infant microbiome.

Enthusiasm has outrun evidence in some quarters, and claims about miracle probiotics deserve scepticism, since the community is highly individual and resistant to permanent alteration by a pill. Yet the direction of the research is clear: human health cannot be understood by the study of human cells alone. We are, as one researcher put it, ecosystems, and medicine is only beginning to learn to tend the whole of them.

gre-r19.title: Animal Cognition
gre-r19.text:
Do animals think? For most of the twentieth century, scientists answered with caution, wary of anthropomorphism, the error of attributing human traits to animals. Behaviourists insisted that animals could be studied only through observable response, and the minds of animals, if they existed at all, were placed beyond the reach of science. That orthodoxy has crumbled. Carefully designed experiments now suggest that many species possess capacities once regarded as exclusively human.

Crows solve multi-step puzzles that human toddlers cannot; some birds cache food and remember thousands of hiding places, tracking what they have stored, where and for how long. Dolphins recognise themselves in mirrors, a test passed by few species and long taken as a sign of self-awareness. Elephants cooperate, great apes appear to attribute beliefs to others, and scrub jays plan for the future, burying food where they will be hungry tomorrow. Even the humble octopus navigates mazes and opens jars with an apparently improvised intelligence.

The researchers who report these findings are careful to avoid claiming human-like minds; a crow is not a small feathered person. Their point is different: intelligence is not a single ladder with humans at the top but a family of solutions to the problem of survival, each beautifully adapted to its own way of life. The study of animal minds has therefore become a study of the many forms thought can take.

gre-r20.title: Mass Extinctions
gre-r20.text:
Life on Earth has not evolved smoothly; its history is punctuated by catastrophes. The fossil record reveals at least five mass extinctions, moments when a large fraction of species vanished within a short geological interval. The most severe, at the end of the Permian period, eliminated perhaps ninety per cent of species, while the most famous, at the end of the Cretaceous, ended the reign of the dinosaurs and cleared the way for mammals.

The causes differ. Some extinctions have been linked to volcanic eruptions on a colossal scale, others to the impact of asteroids, and the discovery of a vast impact crater in the Yucatan peninsula made the asteroid hypothesis for the dinosaur extinction, long resisted, nearly impossible to deny. What matters for the future is that these events altered the entire course of life, and that the recovery times, measured in millions of years, dwarf the span of human civilisation.

Many biologists argue that a sixth mass extinction is now under way, caused not by asteroids or volcanoes but by one species, ours, through habitat destruction, pollution, hunting and climate change. The extinction rate is estimated to be hundreds of times higher than the background level. Unlike earlier catastrophes, this one could in principle be slowed, because its cause is human choice. Whether the choice will be made is not a question for geology but for the political will of the present.

gre-r21.title: Modernism and the Avant-Garde
gre-r21.text:
Modernism was the great artistic rupture of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, a period in which the arts deliberately broke with the conventions that had governed them for centuries. Painters abandoned perspective and realistic likeness; poets abandoned regular metre; composers abandoned tonality. The aim, in the phrase of the poet Ezra Pound, was to make it new, to find forms adequate to a world of industry, war and dissolving belief.

The movement had roots in the experience of a transformed world. The shock of the First World War, the vertiginous speed of new technologies, and the discoveries of psychology, which suggested that the self was not a stable centre but a current of half-conscious impressions, all eroded confidence in the old certainties. Joyce's Ulysses, a single day in Dublin, and Eliot's The Waste Land, a heap of broken images, are among the monuments the impulse produced, works that demanded from readers an entirely new kind of attention.

Modernism was never a single style but a family of declarations of independence, from Cubism to Surrealism, and it generated its own orthodoxy, which later generations would in turn reject. But its deepest legacy is the conviction that art is not bound to imitate what is given, that it may invent its own reality, a conviction so thoroughly absorbed that it is now difficult to imagine art without it.

gre-r22.title: Abstract Expressionism
gre-r22.text:
In the years after the Second World War, the centre of the art world moved decisively from Paris to New York, and the movement that made the transfer unmistakable was abstract expressionism. Its painters, among them Jackson Pollock and Willem de Kooning, abandoned the figure altogether, replacing representation with gesture, colour and the physical record of the painter's action on the canvas. Pollock's drip paintings, made by pouring and flinging paint across enormous canvases laid on the floor, became the movement's symbol.

The critics who championed the movement saw its art as an expression of the individual self in an age of mass conformity, and the Cold War gave the argument a political edge, as American officials promoted the new painting as proof of the freedom of the artist under democracy. Later historians have complicated this story, noting that the artists themselves were often apolitical or leftist, and that the movement absorbed European exiles who had fled fascism.

Abstract expressionism was also attacked, for looking like accidents and child's play, and even its admirers sometimes laughed at its pretensions. Yet whatever one thinks of individual works, the movement permanently changed what a painting could be, insisting that paint itself, its drips and stains, could carry meaning and feeling. It is difficult now to grasp how scandalous that insistence once seemed.

gre-r23.title: The Role of the Art Critic
gre-r23.text:
The art critic occupies an awkward position in the culture of the visual arts: expected to guide public taste, yet frequently accused of failing it. Figures such as John Ruskin and Clement Greenberg shaped entire reputations, championing Turner or demanding that painting attend to its flat surface and paint, and their judgments were read not only by collectors but by artists themselves, who sometimes changed course in response. For most of the modern era, the critic was one of the most powerful figures in art.

The authority of the critic has since diminished. Art criticism was always at risk of seeming parasitic, a profession whose subject is created by others, and the contemporary art world has largely dissolved the old hierarchy. Galleries and museums write their own descriptions, social media supplies instant opinion, and a vast apparatus of curators and advisors now performs the function of interpretation. Some critics have retreated to journalism, others to theory, and the question of what criticism is for has become, ironically, a favourite subject of criticism.

The decline of the critic's power is not, however, the same as the end of critical judgment. Someone must argue about what is good and why, or talk about art degenerates into mere description of preferences. The critic's task, as the best have always understood it, is not to issue verdicts but to give reasons, to make visible qualities that others may then see for themselves.

gre-r24.title: The Birth of Opera
gre-r24.text:
Opera was born around 1600 in Florence, where a circle of poets and musicians, the Camerata, sought to revive the ancient Greek practice of drama sung or declaimed with musical accompaniment. Their experiments produced recitative, a style of singing that follows the rhythms of speech, and the first operas, staged for aristocratic patrons, combined myth, spectacle and music in a new way. Within a century opera had become the most spectacular art form in Europe.

Its rise was inseparable from the courts and cities that commissioned it, and the genre absorbed the ambitions of the age. The monumental opera houses of Venice and Naples made the form public and commercial, and the castrati, singers whose voices could reach extraordinary heights, became celebrities whose fees rivaled those of generals. Handel's London operas and Monteverdi's early masterpieces mark high points, but the form remained, as it still is, a strange alliance of commerce and extravagance.

Critics of opera point out that its conventions are absurd: people do not sing their private griefs at each other for three hours. Yet the absurdity is the point. Song allows emotion to be slowed, amplified and examined, and the combination of music, drama and spectacle can move audiences in ways that spoken theatre cannot match. More than four centuries after its invention, opera remains the great test of the question of what music is for.

gre-r25.title: Cinema as an Art Form
gre-r25.text:
For its first decades, cinema was regarded as a fairground novelty, a mechanical curiosity incapable of art. The early films were short, static and silent, and respectable opinion held that moving images could record but never create. The transformation of cinema into an art form is therefore one of the fastest cultural revolutions on record, accomplished within a generation by pioneers who discovered that the camera could do what the eye cannot.

Editing proved to be the key discovery. By cutting between shots, filmmakers could control time, jump across space and direct attention so precisely that the resulting film, an assembly of fragments, seemed a seamless flow. The close-up revealed faces in a way theatre never could; montage could compress years into seconds or stretch a moment to breaking; and sound, when it arrived in the late 1920s, added new layers of realism and expression. By the 1930s the medium had its own masterpieces, its own criticism and its own theory.

Claims for cinema as the art form of the century are often made and often mocked, but the evidence of its power is everywhere: audiences weep, tremble and are changed by arrangements of light and shadow that are, strictly speaking, nothing but photographs in motion. Whatever its status among the traditional arts, cinema has become the shared visual language of the modern world, and its history is the history of how we learned to see through machines.

gre-r26.title: The Fall of Rome
gre-r26.text:
Few historical questions have been asked more often than why the Roman Empire fell, and none has received more answers. The empire had weathered crises for centuries, and its collapse in the west in the fifth century was not a single catastrophe but a long process of erosion, completed by the entry of Germanic peoples into its provinces. Rome had absorbed invaders before, by incorporating them; this time the machinery of absorption failed.

The explanations advanced by historians form a catalogue of the anxieties of their own ages. Gibbon blamed Christianity and luxury, seeing in the rise of the Church a diversion of energy from civic virtue; others have blamed lead poisoning, inflation, plague, climate change and the sheer cost of defending a frontier that stretched from Britain to the Euphrates. Modern historians are more cautious, treating collapse as a systemic failure in which political crisis, economic strain and military pressure reinforced one another.

The eastern half of the empire, ruled from Constantinople, survived for nearly a thousand years after the west fell, which suggests the empire was not so much doomed as divided. The empire's real legacy was not its fall but its persistence: its law, language, roads, cities and religion outlived its armies and shaped everything that followed, from the Church to the languages of Europe. The question of why Rome fell may be less instructive than the question of why it lasted so long.

gre-r27.title: The Printing Press and the Reformation
gre-r27.text:
The printing press with movable type, developed by Johannes Gutenberg in the 1450s in the German city of Mainz, is routinely ranked among the most consequential inventions in history. Hand-copied manuscripts were expensive, scarce and error-prone; printing made books cheaper, more numerous and more uniform, and it changed who could own them and who could read them. Within fifty years millions of books had been produced across Europe, and literacy and learning expanded with them.

The consequences reached beyond the bookshop. Printed materials carried by merchants and pilgrims spread ideas faster than any network of the past, and vernacular printing strengthened national languages against Latin. Most dramatically, the Reformation of Martin Luther was, in the words of a later historian, a propaganda war conducted largely in print; Luther's pamphlets, printed in vast numbers, turned a theological dispute into a movement that divided Europe. Sovereigns attempted censorship, but presses were portable and borders porous.

Print did not, of course, cause everything that followed; it multiplied voices and messages that already existed. But it changed the conditions under which all subsequent arguments would be conducted, and it offers a standing warning to every age: whoever controls the means of reproduction of ideas shapes the culture. That warning has rarely seemed more current than now.

gre-r28.title: The Industrial Revolution
gre-r28.text:
Beginning in eighteenth-century Britain, a series of technical changes transformed how goods were manufactured and with them the whole texture of human life. The steam engine, the spinning machines, iron-making and later the railway allowed production to move from the cottage and the workshop to the factory, and goods that had been luxuries became ordinary. The Industrial Revolution was the most profound economic transformation since the invention of agriculture.

Its costs were paid at once and in human currency. The new factories demanded long hours of repetitive labour from men, women and children, and the industrial cities grew faster than their sewers, water supplies or housing, breeding disease and discontent. Reformers and workers organised against conditions that now seem barely survivable, and their struggles gradually produced factory acts, trade unions and the modern understanding of labour rights. Meanwhile the countryside, its commons enclosed and its jobs depleted, emptied into the mills.

The long account, however, is not simply a tragedy. Output and productivity rose on a scale without precedent, and real wages, after decades of stagnation, eventually rose with them, as did life expectancy and education. Historians continue to argue over whether the workers of the industrial age gained or lost, a question that cannot be settled with a single balance sheet. What no one disputes is that the revolution remade work, cities and family life and set the pattern for every industrialisation since.

gre-r29.title: Decolonization after 1945
gre-r29.text:
After the Second World War, the European empires dissolved with a speed that astonished their own governments. In 1947 Britain withdrew from India; within twenty years most of Africa and Asia had been decolonised, and by 1975 the Portuguese empire, the oldest, had collapsed in the wake of its African wars. Never had so vast a political structure disappeared so quickly, and the process reshaped the map of the world and the membership of the United Nations.

The causes were many. The war had bankrupted the imperial powers and destroyed their claims to moral superiority, while nationalist movements, often led by a generation educated in the imperial metropoles, had acquired organisation, leaders and mass support. The Cold War added pressure, as both superpowers found reason to oppose old empires. Colonial officials who expected decades more of tutelage found themselves negotiating withdrawal on timetables measured in months.

The aftermath has been mixed and is still unfolding. Some new states inherited functioning economies and built stable institutions; many others suffered from borders drawn in European capitals that ignored ethnic geography, from dependence on a single export and from corruption that the departing powers had sometimes encouraged. The terms decolonisation and postcolonial do not describe a completed event but a continuing condition, and the former empires, transformed by immigration from their former colonies, are themselves being remade by the history they exported.

gre-r30.title: The Great Depression
gre-r30.text:
The Great Depression of the 1930s was the deepest and longest economic contraction in modern history. It began with the collapse of American stock prices in 1929, spreading through a world economy already weakened by war debts and the instability of the gold standard, until industrial production in some countries fell by half and unemployment, in the United States and Germany, reached a quarter of the labour force. Banks failed by the thousands and international trade collapsed.

The causes remain debated. Economists point to monetary contraction, to the fragility of banks, to overinvestment in the 1920s and to the errors of governments that raised tariffs and clung to the gold standard, transmitting deflation from country to country. What is clear is that the slump was not inevitable; policy choices made it deeper and longer, and different policy choices could have shortened it. The lesson of the decade, drawn by economists ever since, is the danger of passivity in the face of a collapsing economy.

The political consequences were severe. Mass unemployment and humiliated pride fed extremism in Germany and Japan, contributing to the catastrophe of the Second World War, while in the United States the New Deal reshaped the relationship between government and economy. The depression's deepest legacy is institutional: the safety nets, deposit insurance, financial regulation and activist central banks created in its shadow, instruments designed to ensure that the world would not relive the 1930s. Whether they are sufficient for the stresses of the present is a question that history has not finished answering.
